title: $\boldsymbol{f}$-OPD: Stabilizing Long-Horizon On-Policy Distillation with Freshness-Aware Control
claim: Asynchronous execution raises throughput but hurts fidelity through stale samples; our freshness-aware control recovers synchronous-level performance at near-asynchronous efficiency.
layout: 2 panels: left timeline schedule diagrams, right Pareto scatter with dashed frontier
description: Panel (a) is a legend-keyed timeline of colored blocks (teacher supervision tan, student rollout red, train blue, policy update green) along a step arrow. The top half shows synchronous OPD with resource groups RG1 and RG2 taking turns, leaving idle gaps. The bottom half shows asynchronous OPD with RG1, RG2 and RG3 pipelined into dense rows of numbered blocks. Blue arrows labeled 'freshness mismatch' link the stale samples. A green arrow and a cloud labeled 'higher throughput' connect the two schedules. Panel (b) is a scatter plot of normalized task performance against relative training efficiency. Blue marks (synchronous) sit at the top left, red marks (asynchronous) sit at the lower right with error bars, and green marks (f-OPD) sit near the top between them. Circles, squares and triangles mark reasoning, tool-use and coding tasks, and a dashed curve shows the frontier. The eye goes first to the colorful block schedule and then to the green points on the plot.
caption: (a) System implementation of OPD under synchronous (top) and asynchronous (bottom) execution. While asynchronous OPD improves training throughput by pipelining computation across multiple resource groups (RGs), the resulting freshness mismatch compromises training fidelity. (b) Performance–efficiency trade-offs across reasoning, tool-use, and coding-agent tasks. Points denote five-seed means with standard deviations. While vanilla OPD executions struggle to simultaneously balance performance and efficiency, f-OPD effectively bridges this gap by freshness-aware control.
abstract: Scaling on-policy distillation (OPD) for large language models (LLMs) confronts a fundamental tension: asynchronous execution is necessary for system efficiency, but structurally deviates from the ideal on-policy objective. To address this challenge, we theoretically decompose the objective discrepancy into rollout drift and supervision drift, capturing staleness in student rollout and teacher context, respectively. Building on this, we introduce a sample-level freshness score that quantifies the reliability of a buffered sample with respect to the on-policy objective. Guided by this signal, we further propose f-OPD, a novel framework that adaptively regulates stale-sample influence and constrains policy drift accumulated under asynchronous training. Across reasoning, tool-use, and coding-agent tasks of increasing interaction horizon, f-OPD consistently achieves task performance comparable to synchronous optimization while largely retaining the throughput advantages of asynchronous execution. Our results establish the first recipe for achieving a performance-efficiency trade-off in OPD, paving the way for long-horizon agentic post-training at scale.
